206.layer4_ar: يتَّفق علماء المذهبين الشيعي والسني على أن الآية تصف الملائكة المقرَّبين وتُقرِّر عبادتهم الدائمة نموذجاً للمؤمنين. وجميع مذاهب الفقه الإسلامي تعترف بسجدة التلاوة عند هذه الآية وإن تباينوا في هل هي واجبةٌ أم مستحبَّة. ويُلحُّ العلماء الكلاسيكيون من الفريقين على المفارقة مع رفض إبليس المتكبِّر للسجود، مستعملين الآية تحذيراً من الكبر وتأكيداً لفضيلة العبادة المتواضعة. ويناقش علماء السنة كالرازي المسألة الكلامية في هل عبادة الملائكة محمودةٌ حقاً لانعدام قدرتهم على العصيان، بينما يرى علماء الشيعة كالطباطبائي أن عبادتهم ذات معنى لأنها تُجسِّد توافق الإرادة الكامل مع الحق. والفريقان يتَّفقان على أن سجود الإنسان عند تلاوة هذه الآية أو سماعها مشاركةٌ في العبادة الملائكية. والتقاليد الصوفية في المدرستين أولت خاصةً عناية للتأمُّل في عبادة الملائكة إلهاماً للسموِّ الروحي الإنساني، مُطوِّرةً ممارسات تأمُّلية في الانضمام الخيالي إلى التسبيح السماوي. ويجد العلماء المعاصرون من كلا المدرستين في الآية أرضيةً مشتركة لتأكيد أهمية العبادة المنتظمة والسجود ترياقاً للكبر والمادية الحديثة.
206.layer1: This final verse of Surah Al-Araf concludes the surah with a majestic image: the angels who are nearest to Allah — the muqarrabun — never allow pride to prevent them from His worship. They glorify Him (tusabbih) continuously, and they prostrate before Him. This verse contains a sajdah tilawah — a prostration of recitation — meaning it is recommended (and according to some scholars, obligatory) to perform a prostration when reciting or hearing this verse. The verse functions as both a description of angelic worship and an implicit invitation to believers to emulate it. If even the greatest of Allah's creation — the angels closest to Him — engage in continuous glorification and prostration, how much more should human beings, who are in constant need of Allah's mercy and forgiveness, do the same? The specific mention of freedom from arrogance ('la yastakbirun') is significant: it was arrogance that led Iblis to refuse prostration and become the first enemy of humanity. The angels' freedom from this vice contrasts sharply with Iblis, making the verse a call to choose the path of humble worship over the path of pride that leads to destruction.
206.layer2: Ibn Kathir in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim explains that 'alladhina inda rabbik' — those near your Lord — refers to the angels, particularly the highest-ranking ones such as the bearers of the Throne and the muqarrabun mentioned elsewhere in the Quran. He notes that 'la yastakbirun an ibadatihi' directly echoes the story of Iblis narrated at the beginning of Surah Al-Araf, forming a literary frame: the surah opened with Iblis's arrogant refusal to prostrate, and it closes with the angels who never commit such arrogance. Tabari in his Jami al-Bayan notes that 'yusabbihunahu wa lahu yasjudun' — they glorify Him and to Him they prostrate — describes two modes of continuous worship: tasbi (glorification through praise) which is constant, and sujud (prostration) which represents the highest point of submission. Qurtubi in Al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran provides detailed discussion of the sajdah tilawah in this verse, noting that this is the first sajdah tilawah in the Quran, and that the scholarly consensus (ijma) holds that it is prescribed for both the reciter and the listener. He also discusses the hadith narrated by Ibn Abbas confirming the prostration at this verse.
206.layer3: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran finds in this verse a fitting conclusion to the entire Surah Al-Araf — a surah that began with the story of human origins, the test of Adam and Iblis, and the long history of prophets and their rejecting nations. The surah ends by lifting the gaze from human history to the cosmic reality: beyond all human struggle and choice, the closest beings to Allah are in unbroken worship. This gives the believer perspective: the purpose of all the guidance delivered through the surah is to bring human beings into alignment with this cosmic worship. Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir emphasizes the therapeutic dimension of the sajdah tilawah commanded by this verse: in prostrating, the reciter enacts the very submission the verse describes, symbolically joining the ranks of those who worship without arrogance. Ibn Uthaymeen reflected that the contrast with Iblis embedded in this verse is the deepest possible motivation for prostration: every time a Muslim prostrates before Allah, he chooses the way of the angels over the way of Iblis, affirming that created beings belong in worship of their Creator. The surah's closing, with this image of angelic devotion, is a call to end every reading of Al-Araf with one's forehead on the ground.
